MINERALS.name: Lithium
profile: The lightest metal, traded mainly as lithium carbonate and lithium hydroxide.
It is the core of lithium-ion battery cathodes and electrolytes, which power electric vehicles, grid storage and backup power for data centres.
Brine deposits in the Argentina–Bolivia–Chile salt flats hold a large share of known world resources, which makes the region central to battery supply chains.

MINERALS.name: Copper
profile: The best electrical conductor among non-precious metals.
Used in wiring, power grids, motors, transformers and the power and cooling systems of data centres; demand rises with electrification and AI infrastructure.
Chile and Peru are the two largest producers in the world. Copper is by far the region’s largest critical-mineral export by value, so it drives the “all minerals” totals.

MINERALS.name: Nickel
MINERALS.note: Ore and ferro-nickel count as general industrial; intermediates and refined nickel count as technology core.
profile: A metal used in stainless steel and in high-nickel battery cathodes (NMC, NCA).
Battery-grade nickel needs refined or intermediate products, which is why the team method splits nickel by stage.

MINERALS.name: Cobalt
profile: Used in battery cathodes and high-temperature superalloys.
Mostly mined as a by-product of nickel and copper; Latin American volumes are small (Cuba is the main source).

MINERALS.name: Rare earths
profile: A group of 17 elements. Neodymium, praseodymium and dysprosium go into the permanent magnets of electric motors, wind turbines and hard drives.
Processing is concentrated in China; its 2025 export controls on rare earths showed why both powers treat new deposits, such as Brazil’s, as strategic.

MINERALS.name: Graphite
MINERALS.note: Flake graphite and synthetic graphite count as technology core; other natural graphite as general industrial.
profile: The main anode material in lithium-ion batteries; also used in refractories and lubricants.

MINERALS.name: Manganese
profile: Essential to steelmaking; also used in some battery cathodes.

MINERALS.name: Niobium & tantalum
MINERALS.note: Tantalum (8103) counts as technology core; ferro-niobium and Nb/Ta/V ores as general industrial.
profile: Niobium strengthens steels and superalloys and is used in superconducting magnets; Brazil dominates world supply. Tantalum goes into capacitors for phones, computers and servers.

MINERALS.name: Molybdenum
profile: An alloying element for steel; in the region mostly a by-product of copper mining.

MINERALS.name: Silver
profile: The most conductive metal; used in electronics and in the conductive paste of solar cells.

MINERALS.name: Zinc
profile: Used mainly to galvanise steel against corrosion.

MINERALS.name: Lead
profile: Used mainly in lead-acid batteries.

MINERALS.name: Tin
profile: The main ingredient of solder, which joins every component on a circuit board.

MINERALS.name: Antimony
profile: Used in flame retardants, alloys and some semiconductors.

MINERALS.name: Tungsten
profile: Used in hard metals for cutting tools and in high-temperature parts.

MINERALS.name: Fluorspar
profile: The source of fluorine chemicals, including battery electrolyte salts and chip-etching gases.

MINERALS.name: Silicon
MINERALS.note: High-purity silicon counts as technology core; metallurgical silicon as general industrial.
profile: High-purity silicon is the base of chips and solar cells; metallurgical silicon goes into aluminium alloys and silicones.

MINERALS.name: Boron
profile: Used in glass, ceramics and neodymium-iron-boron magnets.

MINERALS.name: Aluminium
profile: A light metal for vehicles, power lines and packaging, made from bauxite via alumina.

MINERALS.name: Gallium, germanium, indium
profile: Minor metals used in compound semiconductors, LEDs, fibre optics and displays. Latin American output is minimal.

STEPS.t: One power looks away, the other arrives
STEPS.p: After 9/11, Washington’s attention moved to the Middle East; in Latin America its agenda narrowed to security and trade. The hemispheric free-trade project died at Mar del Plata in 2005. In the same years China joined the WTO and began buying copper, iron ore, soy and oil on a massive scale. In 2001 the US still took 19.4% of the region’s critical-mineral exports, China 5.6%.
By 2010 China took 26.2% of the region’s critical-mineral exports and the US 11.6%. China became Brazil’s top trading partner in 2009, and soon Chile’s and Peru’s.

STEPS.t: One power stumbles, the other lends
STEPS.p: The 2008 crisis started in the United States. China’s policy banks filled the gap, lending tens of billions to Venezuela, Ecuador, Argentina and Brazil, often against oil. Documented US official finance stayed small throughout. The Chinese record stops in 2021; that is missing data, not zero.

STEPS.t: Washington turns inward, Beijing turns owner
STEPS.p: Trump withdrew from the TPP in 2017; NAFTA became USMCA. Washington warned about Chinese influence and created the DFC in 2019. China reduced risky loans and began buying assets: power utilities in Chile and Peru, a stake in SQM in 2018, lithium projects in Argentina. Panama switched recognition and signed the first Belt and Road memorandum.

STEPS.t: Vaccines, lithium and America’s industrial-policy answer
STEPS.p: The technology-core basket leaned towards the US until about 2020 and flipped to China in 2021–22, reaching 43.3% for China against 14.4% for the US in 2024. The Inflation Reduction Act and the Minerals Security Partnership came in 2022, when China was already further along.

STEPS.t: The return of the hemisphere doctrine
STEPS.p: From 2025, pressure replaced partnership offers: Panama left the Belt and Road, tariffs hit friends and rivals, a swap line backed Milei, and US forces entered Venezuela. Yet the 2025 trade data show a division of labour: China buys the ores, the US buys the metal.

A companion study documents 16 cases since 2018 where Washington pressed against a Chinese-linked project. In 7 the Chinese option was cancelled, transferred, frozen or restricted; a US or allied alternative was actually built in 3–4; in 7 nothing observable changed.

The US did not leave; it changed tools, from trade agreements to declarations, warnings, subsidies and finally coercion. China’s toolkit stayed consistent: buy, lend, invest, then build diplomatic ties. The region split: the northern rim is anchored to the US, the South American mineral exporters tilted economically toward China. Governments hedge.

defs: Technology core: lithium, cobalt, rare earths, graphite (flake and synthetic), nickel intermediates and refined nickel, tin, tantalum, high-purity silicon, gallium/germanium/indium. General industrial: copper, aluminium and bauxite, manganese, niobium, molybdenum, silver, zinc, lead, antimony, tungsten, fluorspar, boron, nickel ore and ferro-nickel. Iron ore is context only. Assigned per HS 6-digit code and stage (team list).
Ores and concentrates (raw) and processed products (intermediates, chemicals, refined metal). Downstream goods (batteries, magnets) are outside the export panel.

China; United States; benchmark partners (Canada, EU27, Japan, South Korea); intra-regional (Latin America and the Caribbean); rest of world (including India). In Comtrade years only China, the US and everyone else.
Commitments on the ladder, official finance, and FDI statistics are shown separately and never added together.
Announced → signed, approved or financed → under construction → operating or completed; stalled and cancelled apart. Each status has a dated source (companion study).
Head of state’s ideology (left / centre / right), dated from inauguration; a year takes the orientation in office at mid-year. Team coding for the six focus countries, to verify with two coders.
2001–07 · 2008–14 · 2015–19 · 2020–24 · 2025–, matching the five acts of the team narrative. Each break is still to be justified by a documented event or data break.

Trade: export share, 60% = 1. Official finance: log10(1 + US$ m) scaled so US$30 bn = 1. Diplomacy: rule-based markers. Combined: weighted mean of the available dimensions, with published weights and a sensitivity test.
Absent is never shown as zero: non-reporting countries, years after a source ends (Chinese finance after 2021) and uncoded countries appear grey or “n/a”.
